issues.legal_issue: A will is not proved when the evidence does not establish its execution and attestation.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the finding that the will had not been proved.
The appellants relied only on one attesting witness to prove execution and attestation.
That witness was not present when the testatrix placed her thumb impression on the will and did not see the other attesting witness sign it.
issues.conclusion: The appellants failed to prove the execution and attestation of the will, so the will was not proved; it was unnecessary to decide separately whether it was genuine.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the evidence established execution and attestation of the will. It relied on the testimony of the sole witness offered for that purpose, which did not establish that the other attesting witness signed the will. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenges_will_proof: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which a party challenges a finding about proof of a will.
predicates.sole_attesting_witness_lacks_personal_kn: The only attesting witness relied on to prove the will was not present when the testator executed it.
predicates.witness_did_not_observe_other_attestor_s: The witness did not see the other attesting witness sign the will.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges proof of a will and the only attesting witness lacks personal knowledge of execution and did not see the other attestor sign, the will is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot raise for the first time on appeal a challenge to the opposing party’s status as the next reversionary heirs when the trial proceeded on the contrary footing and no issue on that status was tried.
material_facts: The appellants contended on appeal that a son of one claimant was the reversionary heir.
No issue about the claimants’ status as the next reversioners had been raised at trial, and the trial proceeded on the footing that they held that status.
The trial court refused the appellants leave to file an additional statement raising the issue.
The record did not establish that the alleged son was alive when the limited heir died.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not contend on appeal that the claimants were not the reversionary heirs entitled to succeed to the estate.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the way the case had been pleaded and tried: the claimants’ status as next reversioners was assumed at trial, no issue on that question was raised, and leave to raise it later was refused. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenges_reversionary_sta: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which a party challenges the opposing claimants’ status as reversionary heirs.
predicates.trial_proceeded_on_claimants_being_next_: The trial proceeded on the footing that the claimants were the next reversioners.
predicates.no_trial_issue_on_reversionary_status: No issue about the claimants’ reversionary status was raised for trial.
predicates.leave_to_raise_issue_later_was_refused: The trial court refused permission to add the reversionary-status issue later.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal challenging reversionary status, where the trial proceeded on the claimants being next reversioners, no issue on that status was tried, and permission to raise it later was refused, the challenge is not open.

issues.legal_issue: A court may direct an inquiry into future mesne profits without a specific prayer for them when the suit is for possession of immovable property and mesne profits.
material_facts: The suit sought recovery of possession of immovable property and pleaded an entitlement to an account of mesne profits.
The plaintiffs claimed mesne profits for three years before the suit, valued that claim and paid court fees on it.
The plaint did not specifically ask for future mesne profits, but included a request for such other relief as the court considered fit.
The High Court directed an inquiry into future mesne profits, and the appellants did not contend that the High Court had exercised its discretion improperly or erroneously.
issues.conclusion: The suit fell within Order 20, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the court had discretionary power to direct an inquiry into future mesne profits even though the plaint did not specifically seek them. The Court saw no reason to interfere with the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order 20, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a decree for past and future mesne profits in a suit for possession of immovable property and rent or mesne profits. Past mesne profits require an existing cause of action to be pleaded, specifically claimed, approximately valued and subjected to court fees under Order 7, rules 1, 2 and 7 of the Code and section 7(1) of the Court Fees Act. Future mesne profits have not accrued when the suit is instituted, so they need not be specifically pleaded, valued or fee-paid; in a qualifying suit the court may grant the general relief of an inquiry into them. The Court relied on Basavayya v. Guruvayya, the observations in Fakharuddin Mahomed Ahsan v. Official Trustee of Bengal, and Atchamma v. Rami Reddy; it distinguished Mohd. Yamin v. Vakil Ahmed because that suit did not claim past or future mesne profits or rent.

predicates.suit_for_possession_and_mesne_profits: The proceeding is a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property and for rent or mesne profits.
predicates.plaint_claimed_past_mesne_profits: The plaint claimed mesne profits that had accrued before the suit was instituted.
predicates.specific_future_profit_prayer_absent: The plaint did not specifically request mesne profits accruing after the suit was instituted.

issues.definition: In a suit for possession and mesne profits that claims past mesne profits but lacks a specific prayer for future profits, the court may order an inquiry into future mesne profits.
